For fun, more actual correspondences:

English German Swedish notes
reek Rauch rök G. and S. mean 'smoke'. G. has <ch> /x/ for /k/, finally
tongue Zunge tunga G. has <z> /ts/ for /t/, initially
pepper Pfeffer peppar G. has /pf/ for /p/, initially and /ff/ for /pp/ medially. Originally a Latin loan
worm Wurm orm S. means 'snake'. Initial /wo/ => /o/ happened in Scandinavian
winter Winter vinter some words stay much alike!
hate (verb) hassen hata G. has /ss/ for /t/ between vowels. E. and S. have lost final /n/ in infinitives
daughter Tochter dotter G. has /t/ for /d/, at least initially. E. spelling echoes the earlier fricative sound
year Jahr år Initial /j/ disappeared in some words in Scandinavian

I don't guarantee that the correspondence is exact in all ways.
